title: DDIA 5 · REPLICATION
subtitle: Keep a copy of the same data on several machines: for fault tolerance (a node dies, a copy survives), read scaling (spread reads), and latency (a copy near the user).
footer: Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann). Read the book.

blocks.text: Reads can go to any follower. This is read scaling, but followers may be a little behind: replication lag.
The async follower is updated in the background. It is fast, but if the leader dies now, writes the async follower never got are lost.
If the old leader returns and still thinks it is leader, there are two leaders: split brain. A fix is fencing: shut it down (STONITH) or reject its epoch number (Ch 8).

blocks.text: The fixes give read-after-write consistency: read the user's own profile from the leader; for about 1 minute after a write, route that user to the leader; or have the client remember its last write LSN and read only from a replica that has caught up to it.
Consistent prefix reads: across partitions a reader can see a reply before the message it replies to.
When the changes meet, there is a conflict. Resolution options: last-write-wins (silently loses data), merge values, CRDTs, or ask the user.
Read repair writes the latest value back to the stale node. A background anti-entropy process (Merkle trees) fixes values that are never read.

items: Automated failover promotes a replica (Patroni, RDS Multi-AZ, ~30s).
"User updates a price and refreshes but sees the old price."
Replication lag. Read-your-writes: route that user to the primary for N seconds, or track LSN.
Multi-leader with conflict risk. Prefer a home region per user or hotel, and CRDTs for things like counters.
Leaderless: no failover pause, tunable consistency, write availability during node loss. The cost is conflicts and LWW.
